explain.say: Imagine you grow rice and want fish, but the fisher wants shoes, not rice. Stuck! That puzzle is why people invented money. Look at the board: six steps in the story of money, from swapping to tapping a phone.

explain.say: See barter light up? Barter means swapping goods directly, like rice for fish. It only works if each of you wants what the other has; economists call that a double coincidence of wants. Have you ever swapped snacks with a friend?

explain.say: Next, shells and salt. People began using things everyone valued as money: cowrie shells in Africa, India and China, salt bars in Ethiopia, cattle in many places. Why did shells work so well? Small, tough and hard to fake!

explain.say: Now the coin. About 2,600 years ago in Lydia, in today's Turkey, rulers stamped lumps of precious metal with a set value. No more weighing! Can you guess why a stamp mattered? It promised the value was real.

explain.say: Later came paper money in China, then banks and cards, and today you can pay by phone: M-Pesa in Kenya, UPI in India, Pix in Brazil. Super storytelling! Wow: India's UPI now handles well over ten billion payments every month.

faq.a: Barter is trading goods or services directly without money, like swapping a bag of rice for some fish. It only works when both people want what the other has.
asks: How did people trade before money?

faq.q: Why were shells used as money?
faq.a: Cowrie shells were small, light, tough, hard to fake and easy to count, so they worked well as money across Africa and Asia for centuries.
Some of the earliest known coins were made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 600 BCE, from a gold and silver mix called electrum. Early coins also appeared in China and India.
China did. During the Song dynasty, about a thousand years ago, the government began issuing paper notes called jiaozi, because carrying heavy strings of coins was difficult.
asks: Where was paper money first used?

faq.q: How does paying by phone work?
faq.a: Your phone sends a secure message telling your bank or mobile money account to move money to the seller's account. No cash changes hands; the numbers in the accounts change.

facts: Coins of electrum were made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 600 BCE.
China's Song dynasty issued paper money called jiaozi in the 11th century.
Kenya's M-Pesa launched in 2007; India's UPI launched in 2016; Brazil's Pix launched in 2020.
